title: Ambiguous `filter` Method (Select vs Discard)
pattern: A method named `filter` where it is structurally unclear from the call site whether the closure selects elements to keep or elements to discard.
why_bad: The word "filter" is semantically ambiguous in natural language. A coffee filter removes grounds but keeps the liquid, whereas an air filter removes dust and discards it. Some libraries use `filter` to mean "keep matching" (like Rust's `Iterator::filter`), while others use it to mean "exclude matching". This leads to severe logic inversion bugs.
detection: Custom traits or types implementing a method named `filter` returning a collection, or variables named `filter` without a clarifying prefix.
counterexample:
Standard library iterators where `filter` is highly idiomatic and universally understood to mean "select":
```rust
let active_users: Vec<_> = users.into_iter().filter(|u| u.is_active).collect();
```
fix:
Rename the method or function to `select` or `keep` (if retaining elements) or `reject` or `discard` (if discarding elements) to eliminate ambiguity.
```rust
let active_users = users.select(|u| !u.is_inactive);
```
source: *The Art of Readable Code* by Dustin Boswell and Trevor Foucher (Chapter 3, p. 24, p. 119).
